## Incident Report — MTA 2021-09-10 PCAP Analysis

### Victim Host
| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| IPv4 | **10.9.10.102** |
| MAC | **00:4f:49:b1:e8:c3** |
| Windows hostname | **DESKTOP-KKITB6Q** (NetBIOS/DHCP confirmed) |
| AD domain | angrypoutine.com (DC: ANGRYPOUTINE-DC, 10.9.10.9) |
| Logged-in user | **hobart.gunnarsson** (Kerberos AS-REQ CNameString, both to DC and locally) |

DHCP (frames with option 12) ties hostname `DESKTOP-KKITB6Q` and requested IP `10.9.10.102` to Ethernet source `00:4f:49:b1:e8:c3`; NBNS confirms the same IP answering as `DESKTOP-KKITB6Q<00>`/`<20>` and workgroup `ANGRYPOUTINE`.

### Malware Family
**Attribution: behavioral (no IDS/Suricata alerts were provided in this evidence set — no signature confirmation available).**

The traffic shape strongly matches **Qakbot (Qbot)**-style loader/backdoor behavior:
1. A single HTTP GET to a bare, randomly-pathed URI on a throwaway domain, using a deliberately spoofed/outdated User-Agent (`MSIE 7.0` claiming to run on Windows NT 10.0 — inconsistent with the genuine Edge/Chrome UA seen elsewhere from the same host), returns a PE32+ DLL.
2. Within 4–9 seconds of that download, the host opens repeated TLS 1.2 sessions with **no SNI extension** to two unrelated external IPs, both presenting the identical self-signed certificate (`CN=londonareloeli.uk, O=UK System, OU=LL EST, L=London, C=London`) — a hallmark of Qakbot's rotating raw-IP C2 infrastructure. One of the two IPs was re-contacted **33 separate times** across the capture (persistent beaconing).

I have not verified this against threat-intel sources (no internet access used, per instructions); treat the family name as a behavioral hypothesis, not a confirmed identification.

### Indicators of Compromise (all grounded in this capture)

**C2 endpoints (TLS, no-SNI, shared self-signed cert `londonareloeli.uk`):**
- `167.172.37.9:443` — 1 session, first contact 2021-09-11 03:17:31 UTC+4 (frame 1479)
- `94.158.245.52:443` — 33 sessions, first contact 2021-09-11 03:17:36 UTC+4 (frame 1842), repeated beaconing throughout capture

**Malicious domain / delivery host:**
- `simpsonsavingss.com` → resolved to `194.62.42.206` (DNS A record, frame 1182)

**Malicious URL (payload delivery):**
- `http://simpsonsavingss.com/bmdff/BhoHsCtZ/MLdmpfjaX/5uFG3Dz7yt/date1?BNLv65=pAAS` (GET, frame 1189, dest 194.62.42.206:80, spoofed MSIE 7.0 User-Agent)

**Transferred file:**
- Server-declared filename: `date6` (`Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="date6"`)
- Type: PE32+ DLL (x86-64, GUI subsystem), 284,816 bytes
- **SHA256:** `eed363fc4af7a9070d69340592dcab7c78db4f90710357de29e3b624aa957cf8`
- Extracted via `tshark --export-objects http` and hashed directly from the capture.

### Benign Context (not indicators)
- `download.windowsupdate.com`, `au.download.windowsupdate.com`, `ctldl.windowsupdate.com` (23.1.237.x) — legitimate Windows Update / Defender definition traffic (`Windows-Update-Agent`, `Microsoft-Delivery-Optimization` UAs).
- `store-images.s-microsoft.com`, `www.msftncsi.com`, `login.live.com`, `*.msedge.net`, `nexus.officeapps.live.com`, `settings-win.data.microsoft.com`, `v10.events.data.microsoft.com`, `bing.com`, `update.googleapis.com`, `myexternalip.com` — standard OS/Office/Edge telemetry, connectivity checks, and update traffic from a normally-functioning Windows 10 enterprise workstation.
- LDAP/Kerberos/SMB2/DCERPC/CLDAP traffic to `10.9.10.9` — normal AD domain-join/logon activity for `angrypoutine.com`.

### Incident Summary
The Windows 10 workstation **DESKTOP-KKITB6Q** (10.9.10.102, MAC 00:4f:49:b1:e8:c3), logged in as **hobart.gunnarsson** on domain angrypoutine.com, retrieved a 284 KB PE32+ DLL (SHA256 `eed363fc...957cf8`) via an HTTP GET disguised behind a random URI path (`/bmdff/BhoHsCtZ/.../date1`) from `simpsonsavingss.com` (194.62.42.206), using a spoofed legacy Internet Explorer User-Agent inconsistent with the host's real browser fingerprint. Seconds later the host began repeated no-SNI TLS 1.2 beaconing on port 443 to `167.172.37.9` and `94.158.245.52`, both fronted by an identical self-signed certificate (`londonareloeli.uk`), with 33 connections to the latter over the capture window — consistent with Qakbot-style loader/C2 behavior. Attribution is behavioral only; no IDS alert artifacts were present in the evidence set to provide signature confirmation.
